items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: And met Charles Smith about 1936 I guess.

ctx.x: To your recollection, is Hammond one of the first collectors of early jazz?

He would be one of the earliest that I ever met and that I knew of. But there had been, like Charles Smith had known a few people at Princeton, I know, that had collected records. Probably in the twenties even. Did Charlie Smith go to school with him? I don't know that he went to Princeton either. But there were a few people from there, I remember, that he talked about.
I think Fred Ramsey said that he had, you know, relatively little education. Possibly. But he was, you know, just well educated as far as self-education.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: I know Charles Smith said it's sort of pitiful that Jelly was in the next... And as Charles Smith had told me, it was too brightly lit for a nightclub... Charles had supervised and arranged the sessions... Charles did want me to review it because he knew I liked Jelly.

ctx.x: He received you very ambly, though.

Yeah, very friendly. When Jelly, you see, there was that seniority business, too, that he wouldn't have, Judy, being younger, wouldn't have dared be leader. Once they wanted Jelly to record with Victor, I mean, with Decca, with Louis Armstrong, is what I'm trying to say, when they made that new Arlene's album that Louis made, and Steve Smith also organized that date. The same one that Judy was in, had a band, and the one where they makes the 219 blues. Sidney Bechet was on the date, too. And Jelly was supposed to…
Which place is that now? Music Box. The same place here.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: Charles Smith is mentioned only in the context of correcting a transcription error regarding Buddy Bolden's photo ('Charles Smith got it'), with no indication of a personal or professional relationship with the interviewee.

ctx.x: I have a record he made with Joe Dierensburg. He might have played a little bit after that, not much.

So, because he, I heard. The LARP record? Yeah. It was made about that time, actually. He had cancer, I heard, at that time. He looked in pretty good health and talked like he'd be playing, like he was alright. But a couple years later, maybe about two years ago, he died. So, evidently he did have cancer. And he was one of the better drummers, not flashy in any way either. And maybe in some sense, monotonous compared to some of the other New Orleans drummers, but still a wonderful rhythm section. Buster Wilson…
